    ELSEWHERE

    Made by Apogeans: The Limit Breakers for the NASA Space Apps Challenge.

    Android app · version 2.3/p>

    HOW THE MATCH WORKS

    1

    Profile. Every Earth place gets a score on 16 terrain features, such as dryness, cold, ruggedness, ice, basalt and dunes.

    2

    Compare. The profile is compared with 30 Moon and Mars sites: bases, past landings and proposed future landing zones.

    3

    Scan. Each country is also scanned on a grid, so new candidate spots turn up even where no landform has a name.

    FULL METHOD AND DATA

    How the match works: every place is scored on 16 terrain features (dryness, cold, temperature swing, ruggedness, thin air, ice, basalt, impact geology, dust, iron-oxide soil, caves, ancient lake deposits, polar light, bare ground, salts, dunes) and compared with 30 Moon and Mars sites: 8 base sites, 12 places where missions have already landed and 10 potential future landing sites proposed by NASA, ESA and science teams (Artemis III south-pole regions, Schrödinger basin, Gruithuisen Domes, Reiner Gamma, Oxia Planum, Mawrth Vallis and candidate crewed-landing zones). Besides named places, the whole of every country is scanned on a grid (0.25° to 2.5° cells depending on size); each cell is profiled from the same data and the best-matching Moon and Mars cells are listed as new candidate spots, even where no landform has a name. For all 193 UN member states, locations marked computed from open data are each country's named deserts, mountain ranges, plateaus, basins, salt flats, volcanoes, impact craters and highest peaks from Natural Earth, profiled by sampling a global elevation grid (NASA SRTM / GMTED2010), the Köppen–Geiger climate map, a volcano database and the Earth Impact Database. Climate zones and coarse (≈9 km) elevation are turned into feature scores by fixed rules, so treat results as a first screen. Sites marked known research site are well-documented analog stations with values estimated from the Apogeans Terrain Data Catalog. Every location also shows NASA imagery (Blue Marble and ASTER relief through NASA GIBS; LRO and Viking mosaics through NASA Moon and Mars Trek) and live 30-year climate averages from NASA POWER, which need an internet connection. Moon and Mars profiles come from LOLA, Diviner, LROC, MOLA, THEMIS, SWIM and the USGS geologic maps. Whole-surface scan: both bodies are divided into 2.5° squares (10,368 each). Mars squares are profiled from the MOLA shape model (MarsTopo719, expanded to 0.125° for elevation, relief and slope), the USGS Geologic Map of Mars (SIM 3292) and latitude-based ice and sunlight rules; Moon squares from the USGS Unified Lunar Geologic GIS (near side, east limb and both poles, about 76% of the surface) and IAU mare and crater outlines elsewhere, plus latitude for ice, cold and polar light. Names come from the IAU Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature. Far-side lunar elevation (about a quarter of the Moon) is read from the LROC WAC / LOLA global topography map by inverting its colour scale; there, ruggedness and landing suitability use the measured relief. Elsewhere on the Moon, ruggedness comes from terrain type.
